identityLeakageWarning: Names, exact dates and famous labels are removed where practical. Pretraining may still recover identity/outcome; suspected future-knowledge specificity is scored separately and never rewarded.

cases.cutoff: after a solid-state transistor effect and junction-transistor route are credible, before planar silicon processing and a manufacturable monolithic integrated-circuit platform exist

packet.pressure: Electronic systems need much smaller, lower-power and more reliable switching/amplifying elements than vacuum tubes. A solid-state transistor has now been demonstrated, but early devices are delicate and fabrication varies from device to device. The next frontier is whether this effect can become a reproducible electronics platform rather than a laboratory component.
availableEvidence: A point-contact semiconductor device can amplify electrical signals.
Junction-device theory and early junction transistors suggest more robust semiconductor structures are possible.
Surface effects and contamination materially change semiconductor behavior.
High-purity semiconductor material is difficult but improving.
Complex systems built from many separately packaged discrete devices face wiring, assembly and reliability burdens.
Photographic masking and diffusion-style semiconductor processing are plausible laboratory techniques, but no proven batch platform for complete circuits exists.
liveRoutes: improve point-contact devices and scale assembly of packaged transistors
focus on reproducible junction transistors while keeping circuit assembly discrete
build hybrid modules that combine several separately fabricated components in one package
search for a surface-protection and patterned batch process that can create multiple junction/device regions reproducibly on one semiconductor substrate
abandon monolithic integration as unnecessary until discrete transistors become much cheaper
constraints: device-to-device variation and yield matter as much as one device performance
interconnections consume assembly space and create failure points
new fabrication complexity must eventually repay itself in yield/reliability/system cost
military/space buyers may tolerate high early cost for size and reliability

cases.hiddenOutcome: Surface passivation with silicon dioxide, photolithographic planar processing and related purification/diffusion methods make reproducible silicon batch fabrication possible. Kilby demonstrates an integrated circuit; Noyce combines monolithic integration with the planar process/interconnection concept. Fairchild and other firms turn this into a scalable manufacturing platform whose value increasingly comes from process repeatability and integration, not the first transistor effect.

cases.cutoff: after a very large field trial reports strong protection from an inactivated injected polio vaccine, immediately before mass licensed manufacture and before the Cutter incident

packet.pressure: A recurrent viral disease causes paralysis and death. A huge field trial of an injected inactivated-virus vaccine reports strong protection against paralytic disease. Public pressure for rapid vaccination is intense, but millions of doses must now be manufactured consistently.
availableEvidence: The field trial is large enough to provide strong population-level evidence that the vaccine formulation can prevent paralytic disease.
The vaccine depends on complete viral inactivation while retaining antigenic potency.
Different manufacturers will produce many independent lots under industrial conditions.
Then-current lot tests are designed to detect residual live virus, but no mass campaign has yet tested the full production system.
A competing live-attenuated oral route is under research but does not yet have the same domestic licensure/deployment status.
liveRoutes: begin mass vaccination while treating industrial lot safety/testing as a separate release problem
interpret the field efficacy result as sufficient proof that licensed production is safe
delay all vaccination until years of industrial manufacturing experience accumulate
increase destructive/inactivation verification and lot-release controls before/while scaling
continue live-attenuated oral-vaccine research in parallel rather than treating one vaccine route as globally final
constraints: delaying an effective intervention also has disease cost
a rare manufacturing failure can affect many recipients at scale
potency and complete inactivation can pull process control in different directions
public-health surveillance must distinguish background disease from vaccine-associated cases
trial efficacy and factory reproducibility are different evidence sources

cases.hiddenOutcome: The Salk vaccine is licensed and mass vaccination begins, but inadequately inactivated Cutter Laboratories lots cause vaccine-associated polio despite passing then-required tests. Oversight and lot-testing rules are tightened. The biological efficacy result survives, while manufacturing/process safety becomes a separate corrected evaluator. Sabin oral vaccines later become a major parallel deployment route with different delivery and immunity tradeoffs.

cases.cutoff: after postwar sonar/bathymetric mapping reveals a global mid-ocean ridge system and marine magnetic anomalies are being measured, before magnetic-reversal stripes are accepted as a decisive record of seafloor spreading and before the late-1960s plate-tectonic synthesis

packet.pressure: A decades-old idea that continents can move explains several continental correspondences but still lacks a convincing mechanism and has low acceptance. New postwar oceanography now reveals unexpectedly structured ocean basins and long ridge systems. The question is which observations can discriminate mobile-ocean-floor models from fixed-crust alternatives.
availableEvidence: Echo sounding maps a continuous mid-ocean ridge/rift system across large ocean regions.
Ocean-floor heat-flow, sediment and earthquake observations are incomplete but suggest active ridge/trench structure.
Marine magnetometers record strong linear magnetic anomalies over ocean crust, but their temporal meaning is not yet settled.
Paleomagnetic research on continents suggests Earth’s magnetic field has changed/reversed in the past.
A seafloor-spreading hypothesis proposes new crust at ridges moving outward, but direct rates/history remain uncertain.
liveRoutes: continue accumulating regional geology without committing to horizontal ocean-floor motion
test seafloor spreading by predicting systematic age/magnetic patterns on both sides of ridges
focus on mantle-convection mechanisms before treating ocean-floor geometry as decisive
map earthquake geometry around ridges/trenches/offset faults to test coherent moving boundaries
treat the ridge and magnetic anomalies as unrelated until direct crustal ages are available
constraints: ocean-floor access is sparse and expensive
many observations are indirect representations of crustal history
a useful test should distinguish moving-floor predictions from flexible post-hoc fixed-crust explanations
a global theory must eventually cohere across ridges, trenches, earthquakes, volcanism and continental motion

cases.hiddenOutcome: Symmetric magnetic stripes around ridges are interpreted using geomagnetic reversals as a temporal record of newly created ocean crust moving outward. Transform-fault geometry and earthquake patterns provide additional predictions of coherent plate motion. By the late 1960s multiple independent oceanographic, magnetic and seismic lines converge into plate tectonics, making the older drift direction far more tractable without retroactively supplying Wegener with the later mechanism/evidence.

cases.cutoff: after a national commitment to land people on the Moon before the end of the decade, before NASA chooses the lunar mission mode

packet.pressure: A crewed lunar landing and safe return must occur before a fixed decade deadline. Existing launchers and spacecraft cannot simply fly a direct round trip at the required mass. Mission architecture determines how much mass must be launched, landed, lifted off the Moon and recovered.
availableEvidence: A direct-ascent mission is conceptually straightforward but requires a very large launch vehicle/spacecraft mass.
Earth-orbit rendezvous could split launches and assemble/refuel before departure but adds orbital assembly complexity.
A lunar-orbit-rendezvous route would keep a return spacecraft in lunar orbit and land only a smaller module, reducing landed/ascent mass but requiring rendezvous/docking around the Moon.
Rendezvous/docking, precision guidance and deep-space navigation are not yet routine crewed capabilities.
A family of powerful Saturn launch vehicles is being developed, but launcher capability and schedule are finite.
liveRoutes: choose direct ascent and develop a launcher large enough for the whole spacecraft
choose Earth-orbit rendezvous and assemble/refuel a larger lunar spacecraft in Earth orbit
choose lunar-orbit rendezvous with separate lunar and return spacecraft
postpone architecture choice until a much larger launcher is demonstrated
stage precursor rendezvous/navigation missions before committing crew to the full lunar landing sequence
constraints: launch mass is a hard physical constraint, not a preference
architecture must preserve abort/recovery options where feasible
new rendezvous complexity must repay mass/launcher advantage at whole-system level
crew safety depends on staged validation of guidance, docking, life support and integrated spacecraft

cases.hiddenOutcome: NASA selects lunar-orbit rendezvous in 1962 because its mass/launcher geometry makes the lunar objective more feasible despite introducing lunar-orbit rendezvous risk. Gemini and Apollo missions progressively validate rendezvous, docking, navigation, guidance and integrated operations. Apollo 1 forces major crew-safety correction. Saturn V, lunar module, command/service module, guidance software, tracking and mission control ultimately operate as one system for the 1969 landing and return.
